questions.stem: An 18-year-old man presented with a 3-day history of fever, diffuse abdominal pain, and chest pain. His past medical history included exploratory laparotomy 2 years ago, and he was on no medications. These symptoms have occurred several times over a course of several years. He returned from Turkey 6 weeks previously where he visited relatives. He had a pet cat. On examination, his temperature was 38.6°C. There were signs of peritonitis with rebound tenderness and guarding on abdominal examination. There were discrete erythematous plaques over his shins bilaterally.
questions.lead_in: What is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.explanation: Familial Mediterranean fever FMF is the most likely diagnosis in an 18-year-old of Turkish descent, with fever, peritonitis, and previous laparotomy, suggesting recurrence of symptoms. Erysipelas-like lesions on the lower legs may be experienced by 15%–20% of patients. There is a very low risk of malaria in Turkey, and antimalarial prophylaxis is not recommended. Malaria would not be expected to cause a skin rash. Yersinia enterocolitica and Yersinia pseudotuberculosis may cause acute yersiniosis. This usually manifests as fever, abdominal pain, and diarrhea, which have often been present for at least 1 week before the patient seeks help. Bartonella henselae infection would typically present either with skin changes at the primary inoculation site or with regional lymphadenopathy. It can manifest as a fever of unknown origin or with abdominal pain secondary to granulomatous involvement of the liver and/or spleen.
questions.source: Comprehensive Review of ID · Quiz 1 Q47

questions.stem: A 42-year-old man presented with a 3-week history of fever associated with progressive low back pain, malaise, nausea, vomiting, and diarrhea. He had a history of asthma, for which he used regular low-dose steroid inhalers. He was not on any oral medications and had no known drug allergies. He worked in an office. He had sustained a cut to his finger 6 weeks previously while on a hunting trip that involved slaughtering, cooking, and eating wild boar. None of his friends became sick although he said that their wilderness guide had been coughing during their entire trip. On examination, his temperature was 38.9 oC. He had hepatosplenomegaly on abdominal palpation. There was some mild epididymo-orchitis on genital exam. His respiratory and cardiovascular exams were unremarkable. Investigations: Total white cell count 2.5 ×109/L Hemoglobin 8.2 g/dL Platelet count 90,000/μL Computed tomography scan of his abdomen and pelvis demonstrated enlarged liver and spleen and also showed evidence of sacroiliitis.
questions.lead_in: What was the most likely route of acquisition of his infection?
questions.explanation: Direct contact This is a two-stage question, requiring you first of all to identify what the infection is most likely to be and then how the patient has acquired it. This is a case of acute brucellosis, compatible with the exposure history and clinical findings of fever/sacroiliitis/hepatosplenomegaly and pancytopenia. Genitourinary symptoms may also be seen. The incubation period is usually a week to a month but may be much longer. Brucella spp. may be found worldwide, and on average 100–200 cases are reported annually in the United States. The highest number of cases are reported from California, Texas, Arizona, and Florida. Brucellosis has multiple routes of acquisition: direct contact, inhalation of aerosol from an infected animal, ingestion of unpasteurized milk, blood transfusion, and organ transplantation. There is no personto-person transmission. Infection also does not occur after an arthropod bite or ingestion of cooked meat. Hunters may be particularly at risk through coming into contact with the blood and organs of the hunted animals, such as wild boar, elk, moose, and deer. Vets and slaughterhouse workers may also be exposed occupationally.
questions.source: Comprehensive Review of ID · Quiz 6 Q18

parts.text: What 4 phenotypic tests are level 2 (sentinel) labs allowed to do for preliminary workup of Brucella (a Gram stain aside)?
What are 4 things you can do in the laboratory to prevent lab-acquired transmission?

parts_raw.text: What 4 phenotypic tests are level 2 labs allowed to do for preliminary workup of Brucella (cannot use gram stain)?
What are 4 things you can do in the lab to prevent lab-acquired transmission?

questions.model_answer: a) (1) Colony morphology on sheep blood agar (tiny, non-hemolytic, slow-growing after >48 h); (2) catalase (positive); (3) oxidase (positive); (4) urease (positive, often rapid). (No/failure to grow on MacConkey is also used as a screening feature.) b) (1) Handle all manipulations of suspect isolates in a certified biosafety cabinet using BSL-3 practices; (2) never sniff/subculture plates on the open bench; avoid aerosol-generating procedures (vortexing, catalase on open slide); (3) wear appropriate PPE (gown, gloves, respiratory protection); (4) notify/refer to reference lab, restrict access, and provide post-exposure prophylaxis and serologic monitoring for exposed staff.
questions.beyond_mandell: Sentinel/level-2 lab workup steps and biosafety measures are from ASM Sentinel Level Clinical Laboratory Guidelines / CDC Brucellosis Reference Guide; the pp. 2755-2757 slice notes only that brucellosis is among the most common lab-acquired infections via airborne route.

questions.question: The microbiology laboratory director calls you. Several of his technicians worked with an isolate of Brucella species on open benches.
questions.question_raw: 34. The microbiology laboratory director gives you a call. Several of his technicians worked with an isolate of Brucella spp. on open benches.

parts.text: Name three specific manipulations that would put a technician at high risk of laboratory-acquired Brucella.
Name three elements of your management plan for the technician with high-risk exposure.

parts_raw.text: Name 3 specific manipulations that would put a technician at high risk of laboratory acquired Brucella.
b) Name 3 elements of your management plan for the technician with high risk exposure

questions.model_answer:
a) (1) Aerosol-generating manipulation of the growing culture on the open bench — vortexing, sonicating, subculturing, or centrifuging without sealed carriers. (2) Sniffing the culture plate, or performing catalase/oxidase, Gram stain, biochemical or identification testing (including MALDI-TOF extraction) on the open bench. (3) A spill or breakage of the culture outside a biological safety cabinet, or a percutaneous/mucous membrane exposure (needlestick, splash to eyes/mouth) or direct skin contact without gloves.
b) (1) Post-exposure prophylaxis for 3 weeks: doxycycline 100 mg PO BID plus rifampin 600 mg PO daily (TMP-SMX plus rifampin if doxycycline is contraindicated, e.g. pregnancy). (2) Symptom surveillance with twice-daily fever self-monitoring for 6 months (at minimum for the first 6 weeks) and instructions to present immediately for blood cultures if febrile. (3) Baseline serum for serology, banked, with follow-up Brucella serology at 6, 12, 18 and 24 weeks; notify all exposed workers and public health/laboratory management, complete an exposure risk assessment classifying high vs low risk, and review biosafety practices so that suspect isolates are handled in a BSC at CL3.
questions.beyond_mandell: CDC guidance on Brucella laboratory exposures (2008/2012 risk classification, PEP and 24-week serologic follow-up).

cohort_answer.text: High-risk manipulations: Generation of aerosols (centrifugation without sealed carriers, vortexing, sonicating without BSL-3 precautions); Spill at the bench; Smelling the colony plate; Direct contact without gloves and touching face/mucous membranes. Management: Antibiotic prophylaxis (doxy+rifampin or TMP-SMX+rif) x3wks; Symptom watch, daily fever check x24wks (6mo); Serology at 0,6,12,18,24 weeks post exposure. CDC guidance details exposure classification (high/low risk), PEP recommendations, and follow-up monitoring for lab exposures.

parts.text: Why do you need to notify the microbiology laboratory?

parts_raw.text: Why do you need to notify the microbiology laboratory?

questions.model_answer: a) Brucella is one of the most common laboratory-acquired infections (largely airborne); notification lets the lab handle the isolate under BSL-3 precautions, avoid aerosolizing manipulations, and institute post-exposure prophylaxis/serologic monitoring for exposed staff. b) (1) Skeletal/osteoarticular system (most common, up to ~50% of cases); (2) nervous system (neurobrucellosis, ~10%) [genitourinary involvement 5-10% is the next most frequent]. c) (1) Doxycycline; (2) rifampin; (3) an aminoglycoside (streptomycin or gentamicin); (4) trimethoprim-sulfamethoxazole (ceftriaxone is added for neurobrucellosis).
questions.beyond_mandell: The lab-notification/biosafety rationale is CDC/ASM sentinel-lab guidance; the slice supports that brucellosis is a leading lab-acquired airborne infection.

questions.question: A Brucella plate was manipulated on an open bench in the laboratory.
questions.question_raw: Brucella plate manipulated on open bench.

parts.text: Name three aspects of management of a high-risk exposure.

parts_raw.text: Name three high-risk activities in lab.
Name 3 aspects of management of high risk exposure

questions.model_answer:
a) (1) Manipulating an open Brucella culture plate on an open bench outside a biosafety cabinet, or being within about 5 feet of such manipulation. (2) Procedures that aerosolize the organism performed outside a biosafety cabinet - vortexing, centrifuging without sealed carriers, catalase testing, subculturing/streaking, or sniffing plates. (3) Direct personal inoculation or mucosal exposure - needlestick or sharps injury, direct skin contact with a culture (especially non-intact skin), mouth pipetting, or spray/splash into eyes, nose, or mouth.
b) (1) Risk assessment: identify and stratify all laboratory workers present as high- versus low-risk exposures, notify the laboratory director, occupational health, and public health, and confirm the isolate identity/biosafety-level-3 handling going forward. (2) Post-exposure prophylaxis for all high-risk exposures: doxycycline 100 mg PO BID plus rifampin 600 mg PO daily for 3 weeks, started promptly; substitute TMP-SMX DS BID for rifampin if the strain is rifampin-resistant (e.g. RB51) or rifampin is contraindicated; TMP-SMX-based regimens are used in pregnancy and young children. (3) Symptom surveillance and serologic follow-up: instruct workers to report fever or compatible illness and check temperatures for 6 months; obtain baseline serum and repeat Brucella serology at 6, 12, 18, and 24 weeks post-exposure, with blood cultures and treatment for symptomatic seroconversion. Low-risk exposures receive surveillance and serology, with PEP considered if immunocompromised or pregnant.
questions.beyond_mandell: CDC MMWR 2008;57(2):39 laboratory Brucella exposure guidance (risk tiers, PEP regimen, 24-week serologic schedule).

cohort_answer.text: High-risk exposure defined as: 1) direct personal exposure (sniffing cultures, direct skin contact, mouth pipetting, inoculation, spraying into eyes/nose/mouth); 2) working on open bench with open Brucella culture plate or close proximity (across open bench or within 5 feet); 3) presence during procedures that might aerosolize organisms (vortexing, catalase testing). Low-risk = present in lab during exposure but not meeting high-risk definition. Management: Step 0: risk assessment for all exposed workers; Step 1: offer PEP to all high-risk exposures (Doxycycline 100mg BID + rifampin 600mg daily x3 weeks, unless rifampin-resistant strain then add TMP-SMX DS BID to doxy; can give PEP to low-risk exposure if immunocompromised/pregnant, sometimes up to 6 months post-exposure); Step 2: surveillance for symptoms x6 months; Step 3: serologic follow-up (baseline, 6, 12, 18, 24 weeks post-exposure). (MMWR Morb Mortal Wkly Rep. 2008;57(2):39)

parts.text: Name 2 bacteria found in aerobic and anaerobic blood culture that grow on sheep blood agar but not on MacConkey agar.

parts_raw.text: 2 bacteria that are in aerobic and anaerobic blood culture that grow on sheep blood agar but not on MacConkey?

questions.model_answer: (1) Brucella spp; (2) Francisella tularensis. (Other fastidious gram-negative coccobacilli that grow on sheep blood but not MacConkey include Actinobacillus, Eikenella corrodens, Haemophilus, and Campylobacter.)
questions.beyond_mandell: This microbiology fact is from standard clinical microbiology (Manual of Clinical Microbiology); the pp. 2755-2757 slice does not cover primary isolation media.

cohort_answer.text: Eikenella corrodens; Actinobacillus spp; (also considered: Campylobacter, Brucella). GNB aerobic bacilli that will not grow on MacConkey: Actinobacillus, Gardnerella, Brucella, Francisella, Eikenella, Haemophilus, Campylobacter, Legionella, Bordetella, Helicobacter

questions.question: Bacterial culture characteristics: serologic diagnosis.
questions.question_raw:
Q65 (2012 AM, 2011 AM)
Bacterial culture characteristics
questions.model_answer: Serology detects antibodies against Brucella as indirect evidence of infection. The serum agglutination test (SAT/Wright reaction) is the reference method, positive at a titer >=1:160; the rose-bengal slide agglutination test (RBT) is a rapid affordable screening card test. The Coombs antiglobulin test detects non-agglutinating antibodies (serial dilutions needed to overcome prozones), and immunocapture ELISA (Brucellacapt) and standard ELISA are comparable to conventional tests. CDC warns that positive ELISA results must be confirmed by standard agglutination. Negative serology does not exclude disease (use >1 test), and antibodies persist after recovery, so IgG avidity testing helps distinguish active from past infection.

cohort_answer.text: Serology = testing serum for antibodies against a particular organism to indirectly test for presence of recent/previous exposure. IgM – recent, acute exposure. IgG – convalescent serology (more remote exposure)

questions.question: Bacterial culture characteristics: molecular diagnosis.
questions.question_raw:
Q65 (2012 AM, 2011 AM)
Bacterial culture characteristics
questions.model_answer: PCR detects Brucella DNA and is satisfactory in symptomatic patients with negative serology, recognizing disease as early as 10 days after inoculation and useful during outbreaks or relapses. It supplements culture and serology in the overall diagnostic assessment.

cohort_answer.text: Test for presence of bacterial DNA indicative of a particular organism
